lines.text: Silk Road merchants, Persian poets and great scholars, then empire, civil war and the high Pamirs. This is the story of Tajikistan.
More than five thousand years ago, people built Sarazm, one of the oldest towns in Central Asia.
By the sixth century BCE, Persian was being carved in stone. A form of it is still the language of the Tajiks.
At the same time, the land was part of Sogdia, whose merchants carried goods and ideas along the Silk Road all the way to China.
After the Arab conquest, the Samanids, a Persian dynasty ruling from Bukhara, brought a golden age to the region.
At their court the poet Rudaki wrote verse that earned him the title father of Persian poetry.
Avicenna, born near Bukhara, became a physician and philosopher whose Canon of Medicine was taught for centuries.
Centuries later, after Russian and Soviet rule, Emomali Rahmon was born in 1952. He would lead the country for decades.
In 1976 work began on the Rogun Dam on the Vakhsh River, planned to be the tallest dam in the world.
In 1991 the Soviet Union collapsed, and Tajikistan, a land of mountains, became independent.
Within a year civil war broke out, and it would last until 1997.
Amid the turmoil, the Tajik National Park was created to protect the Pamirs, now a World Heritage Site.
From Sogdian traders to the roof of the world, Tajikistan carries a Persian heritage into its future.
